comments.author: duck_tape
comments.text:
Nice post. I really feel all of that right now as well.

Regarding that last Andreas quote at the end, something that I don't think we've come to terms yet is that a lot of our learning was happening incidentally, as part of our everyday tasks. You couldn't help but learn while you were implementing some random feature, or doing the yak shaving to set up CI for a new compilation target, etc.

And now, we can magic those bits away. We can just "create" whatever is in our head. But we can't just incidentally learn anymore. It's actually really hard to stay engaged while the LLM churns through a bug for you.

I don't know what the conclusion of this is. But I don't think that saying "I actually like coding by hand" will be virtue signaling, any more than saying "I like to lift weights" is virtue signaling. You have to put in some time somewhere now to learn and get better.

comments.author: bmo
comments.text: It's easy for someone like Andreas to pivot to using LLMs because he has built up the skill to ensure they're doing quality work and solving the right problems, and that's not going to atrophy immediately. But I don't know how the next generation of programmers ever gets there if they have LLMs from the outset, and the simple types of work that build skill are also the easiest to automate away. As an industry we are collectively shooting ourselves in the foot.

Not sure if the skill mix they acquire this way is the best one, and this surely shifts the skill mix, but when have we ever  known what is the best skillset to be acquired!

comments.author: gered
comments.text:
The part about scrolling past a lot of news stories / links to things people have shared really resonates with me. I've found myself doing the same. In the somewhat rare case that I actually click through to some Github repository, when I notice a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md or similar, I instinctively find myself closing the tab. Whatever interest I might've had in the project just evaporates immediately ... not even a conscious thought anymore I would say. Perhaps that's a bit sad.

Like ... on a purely technological level, I do believe that it is kinda magical that LLMs can do this type of stuff, to the extent that they are currently able to, despite their obvious flaws. That vibe-coding is even possible to the extent that it is.

But I just don't care about people making new projects this way. It's not interesting to me. From what I see in my own day-to-day, the people working this way aren't really learning that much from it either (not to say they learn nothing, but in my experience it absolutely pales in comparison to pre-LLM times), and they mostly don't seem to feel attached at all to anything they create this way either. Most things seem to be almost throw-away efforts now. But not everything.

I feel this way too about my own vibe-coded creations, in the few times that I've tried it myself. I come away from it not really caring, and definitely not having a solid understanding of what I had the LLM spit out.

A big part of why I enjoy software development is the joy of building complex systems myself and understanding how they work, and especially, the feeling of satisfaction I get when I've built something complex that works well. Even if no one ends up using it. When I use LLMs to assist in software development, I find they just rob me of this satisfaction, almost entirely. I almost feel "dirty" afterwards.

I learned to program as a kid and have done it literally as long as I can remember. I feel compelled to make things and have always looked up to people like OP who do things that are difficult because they have the same urge that I do.

Using an LLM robs you of this and I don't have the same respect for it. It's not about what you produce at all. I want to celebrate when someone writes the thousandth NES emulator, even though no one will likely use it, because they harnessed some inner passion to grapple with a challenge that was unfamiliar to them, and came out stronger for it, and we have the evidence that they succeeded. You're probably not going to add much novelty in your implementation, but it's yours, and you've proven yourself to be the type of person who could make it. Using an LLM to generate an NES emulator on the other hand is entirely pointless, because there are already many of them and you learn little that way.

I hope people keep practicing the craft even if everyone who never had that passion deserts it. It's one of the things that makes the world beautiful to me.

the whole point of coding by hand is the enjoyment of the act of doing it.


Agreed. That's where the chess metaphor falls short, as you simply can't play alone just for the sake of it.

Another good metaphor could be acoustic VS. e-bikes.

There's no debate that e-bikes will get you farther than acoustic bikes, and yet there's still a lot of people (myself included) riding conventional bikes "for the sake of it". And these people usually get frustrated when they get overtaken by an e-bike, even though there's no competition or any kind of stakes, and that this choice should only be about what makes them happy and not what other people do. I used to be like that too, and that's because I was passionate about it and couldn't understand why people would "cut corners" like that. I've now overcome it, and I have no issue with other people riding e-bikes as I know WHY I don't do it myself. I've yet to reach the same state with AI though, haha (but I'm making progress, I promise !).

However, the proliferation of e-bikes had a REAL impact on cycling as a hobby that should not be ignored, and that's lowering the skill ceiling so much, that it spoils the fun for conventional riders.

I do participate in multiple XC events (basically trailing on a bike). They're not competitions, just circuits of different length, open to anyone. The hardest/longest ones (50 to 80km) used to be for top-tier riders, because they require a lot of training and confidence to complete. Not many people engaged in this circuits, because even 50km is a lot when you're only a seasonal rider. I personally love it because it challenges me both physically, technically and mentally.
However now that e-bikes are the norm, newcomers tend to engage on these circuits because the distance isn't that much when you're assisted. The problem is that endurance is not the only skill required there, and they usually end up walking/pushing their bike in most technical sections. This ruins the experience for "conventional" riders, because even though they are ready for it, they must stop so many times mid-section because of e-bike people riding too slow, walking in descents, or pushing in technical ascents. I try my best not to be a hater, be tolerant and so on, but it really kills the fun.

And I can see the same problem arising for hobbyist programming: you wanna build a project "the artisanal way", but every single framework/library you might need or even the toolset, your editor/IDE, etc… is geared toward AI-assisted coding. This would ruin the fun for you.

And yeah I agree a hobbyist's laptop is not means of production. But a wage worker's laptop that they own is also not what makes them petty bourgeois. They still sell their labor power to a capitalist. Hence why you are still part of the proletariat.

comments.author: cole-k
comments.text:
Posts like these have had me thinking recently about what makes art good. Art in this case being things we create because they give us purpose, like the author's retrocomputing project.

My working theory is that good art is original. Which means something that (1) no one else has done before or (2) no one else can do.

So for (1) someone can appreciate Starry Night as painted by Van Gogh, but if I make a perfect copy of it they're probably not going to be as impressed. It's not simply the painting itself that is an achievement --- the art exists in the context of our society. For (2), if someone thinks a water fountain is amazing, they probably would still be amazed if I were to make an exact copy of it, simply because making water fountains is hard.

(I think these qualities are not binary: this someone might still be impressed if you could perfectly recreate Starry Night if it were hard e.g. in the time before cameras)

The author's retrocomputing project's value as art laid chiefly in (2) --- this is not to say that no one can do it, but it needs time and care that no one but the author will put in. Now with the advent of LLMs, simply thinking "what if we had X" is basically enough to (possibly) create X. (There are people who will appreciate the craftsmanship, and I agree that a drive-by LLM creation will likely lack a "human touch," but it still dilutes the value of the final human product IMO) So what began as a quest for the author to create X now feels hollow.


I think this also explains why AI-generated menus and websites aren't as impressive as they might initially seem. Let's be generous and assume that they are aesthetically better than whatever came before. The problem is that now everyone is making them and the LLM tells are becoming obvious. So we're in a world where (a) we (think we) can tell apart a beautiful LLM menu and a beautiful human menu and (b) making the beautiful LLM menu is a prompt away. If everyone could summon Van Gogh to paint them some variation of Starry Night --- and they then hung them up in their living rooms --- something would be lost by the time you see the fiftieth Starryish Night.

My suspicion is that art will persevere by pushing further into the "out of distribution." I presume this is already what happens with the avant garde. It will be a sad day if we ever cease creating what the machine cannot.

comments.text:
What vibecoding does is lift the average complexity of software much higher. The 10k line program of last year which might have taken months to code can be done in a day. Now the 100k line program even with vibecoding still takes months of work. So the new standard is the 100k line program.

As someone who programmed by hand for 30 years but have also been building coding agents since 2021 I can say it's still pretty hard to make quality software. My most recent open source project is Abject, which I used claude to build and it still has taken a lot of work. It's such a weird project that I am constantly fighting the LLM because it's built in a way that normal software isn't. Work just shifted to testing and reviewing code and of course planning and plan iterations.

I'm just as satisfied building Abject as I was building Firestr back in 2014 by hand. I'm also using Abject daily where Firestr never got to the point where I could.

At the same time, I have empathy for people who want to craft code by hand as I did for 30 years. Software craftsman movement will continue.

comments.author: zem
comments.text:
this is about where I am, I'm almost 100% coding with claude now, but also I'm taking a lot of time and trouble to make sure the resulting code is human maintainable by looking over the output, making sure I understand what is going on, and directing claude to rework and refactor if it doesn't look satisfactory. I still feel the sort of satisfaction I got from writing the code by hand because for me the satisfying bit is the clean, readable source code and architecture.

e.g. in one of my current projects I got claude to churn out a desktop app, then looked at the code and suggested ways to rewrite it using a model-view-presenter pattern, then derived a "command language" that let UI events be accepted over a socket and then used that to drive both the test harness and an undo/redo framework. the code now fits my vision of what I would like it to look like very well, and I got there in less time than doing it by hand would have been. I also didn't really want to have to learn the fine details of how to configure qt widgets and interface the event loop with a network server or background worker threads; if I were doing that myself I would likely be copying code from existing projects or stackoverflow anyway.

comments.text:
Very well-written article. I really like how he's able to draw distinctions, e.g., between AI tools versus the industry or the general malaise.


it did cause me to question why I bother writing software for 40-year-old computers that only gets used by a handful of people and why I'm bothered by vibecoded software in this context.


I had a similar crisis of meaning, though it was several years ago and in a different retrocomputing community. A legacy codebase got reverse engineered, which was a brilliant achievement that I still think is a wonderful thing. But someone else forked the code soon after that, and the community shifted towards the fork, and that left me feeling untethered. Why am I still drawn to the old, buggy program? Why does no one else seem to care? Why do I hate this one friggin' fork so much?

All of that unfolded pre-AI, which made it a really interesting emotional experience, uncomplicated by debates about plagiarism or water usage or business practices or any other external factors. To replicate the emotions, all you really need is to invest your identity in something, and then have that something pulled out from under you.

I don't have any magic answers. But I heartily endorse being intentional about pondering these things! Just because your source of meaning is lost or has changed doesn't mean you can't find it again.

comments.author: flipGimble
comments.text:
I find that people who are most disillusioned by AI advances are those who love software development and computers for their own sake, and in many cases most of their identity is bound up with computers with little beyond that. I was this type of person through out my 20s and 30s, so no insult to anyone. I would start projects like writing a game engine for example, just because they were fun, or educational, with little thought of their purpose beyond that. I took pride in the craft of coding, and fulfillment in learning obscure technical topics.

There are others however for whom computers are a tools to enable other pursuits and solve problems that have meaning beyond just the digital world. I know artists who are using AI to experiment on interactive 3d visualizations for music concerts and art installations. They can go way beyond what their skills let them do previously. I know a grandmother that built some shopify store fronts and is now vibecoding the coolest looking herbalism inventory management system for one person. They are, perhaps naively, excited about what AI allows them to do.

I'm reflecting that I need to change my perspective and ask what do I want to solve in the real world that is now possible thanks to this new electric powered bike for the mind. That seems a more fulfilling approach that bemoaning that my knowledge of an obscure graphics framework is now a 2min demo for a frontier llm.
